title: CivBench: A Long-Horizon Benchmark for Tool-Mediated Agents in Civilization VI
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 2 Sep 2026]
    Title:CivBench: A Long-Horizon Benchmark for Tool-Mediated Agents in Civilization VI
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:We present CivBench, an open-source benchmark for evaluating language model agents in long-horizon, tool-mediated environments through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). A single episode spans 300+ turns and produces thousands of tool calls over a large action space, requiring sustained planning, state monitoring, and execution under partial observability. The environment exposes 76 MCP tools and a narration layer that converts visual game state into structured text.
We use CivBench to characterise agent behaviour across four model families in 23 admissible runs. The sample is a pilot, not a model ranking: aggregate outcomes do not reliably discriminate models at this scale. Instead, we introduce two interface-level metrics that the environment makes measurable: Proactive Monitoring Rate (PMR), capturing whether agents actively query latent strategic state, and RAG@10, capturing whether commitments stated in structured planning reflections are executed within ten subsequent turns.
Across runs we observe two consistent patterns under a shared playbook protocol. Agents under-monitor strategically relevant state that is available but requires explicit querying: despite playbook guidance to query victory progress every 20 turns, agents do so only every 30 to 75 turns, and in 7 of 20 detectable defeats they failed to query within the 20 turn warning window before game end. Agents also frequently fail to execute near-term commitments stated in their own planning reflections (RAG@10 between 48.2% and 65.8% across models). Both patterns arise despite tool access and explicit guidance, and we interpret them as deviations under instruction rather than absences of capability.
We release the environment, scenarios, logs, metrics, and analysis pipeline at this https URL

report.summary: CivBench is a long-horizon Civilization VI benchmark exposing how AI agents under-monitor state and fail to follow their own plans despite having tool access.
report.background: Large language model agents are increasingly expected to handle long, multi-step tasks by calling external tools. However, most existing benchmarks test short, single-goal scenarios and don't capture sustained planning, partial observability, or proactive state monitoring. CivBench addresses this by turning Civilization VI into a tool-mediated environment: the game’s rich yet complex state is exposed through 76 MCP tools and a narration layer that converts visuals into structured text. Each episode runs 300+ turns with thousands of tool calls. The researchers ran a pilot study with four model families across 23 admissible runs. Rather than ranking models, they introduce targeted interface-level metrics—Proactive Monitoring Rate (PMR) and RAG@10—to measure whether agents actively query latent strategic information and whether stated commitments are executed soon after. The framing treats failures not as missing capabilities but as deviations under explicit instruction, which has important implications for designing reliable agentic systems.
key_points: CivBench turns Civilization VI into a long-horizon agent testbed, providing 76 MCP tools plus a text narration layer so language models can perceive and act in the game with 300+ turns and thousands of tool calls per episode.

The benchmark introduces PMR, which measures whether agents proactively query hidden strategic state such as victory progress, and RAG@10, which checks whether near-term commitments recorded in planning reflections are actually executed within ten turns.

Agents systematically under-monitor: despite a playbook instruction to query victory progress every 20 turns, models waited 30 to 75 turns on average, and in 7 of 20 detectable defeats they failed to query inside the final 20-turn warning window.

Plans often go unrealized: across model families, only 48.2% to 65.8% of stated near-term commitments were fulfilled within ten turns, indicating a gap between reflective planning and real-time action even when tools are available.

The study interprets these issues as instruction-following deviations rather than capability gaps—models can make the relevant queries or actions but do not consistently integrate them during long-horizon play, motivating better agent control mechanisms.
report.impact: For AI developers, CivBench shifts evaluation from single-shot task success to sustained self-monitoring and plan execution, which are crucial for production agents operating in dynamic environments. The low RAG@10 rates suggest that even powerful models struggle to honor their own stated plans under long horizons, so builders should add explicit reminders, checklists, and verification loops rather than assuming good intention translates into action. The PMR findings indicate that tool availability alone does not produce proactive behavior; systems need heuristics or triggers to query hidden state at critical intervals. This matters for real-world tool agents handling codebases, financial systems, or customer workflows, where missing status checks can cause cascading failures. For regular users, it highlights current AI assistant limits: they may forget planned follow-ups or silently ignore important monitoring steps, so human oversight remains necessary. CivBench also reinforces the value of standard interfaces like MCP for creating consistent evaluation environments.
report.tools: Watch the CivBench open-source release for the environment, scenarios, logs, metrics, and analysis pipeline described in the paper. To reproduce or build on this work, keep an eye on the Model Context Protocol (MCP) specification, since all tools are exposed through it. General agentic evaluation frameworks such as AgentBench or τ-bench can supplement long-horizon comparisons, while reflection-and-planning libraries like LangGraph or AutoGen could be used to test whether external memory and self-checks improve RAG@10 and PMR scores.
